---

## The 5-Day Gap Is Significant

In England in 1865, burial typically followed death within 3–7 days. The gap between **3 June** and **8 June** fits that window almost perfectly. The most common explanation for this exact pattern is:

- **One date = death**, **the other date = burial**
- A later informant (or a gravestone engraver, obituary writer, or family member) confused the two

## Evaluate Each Record on Three Axes

| Question | Record A (3 June) | Record B (8 June) |
|---|---|---|
| **Source type** | What kind of record? (civil reg, parish, coroner…) | Same question |
| **Who was the informant?** | Present at the death? Or reporting later? | Same question |
| **When was it created?** | Days after death, or years later? | Same question |

A **civil death registration** filed within days by someone present at the death outranks a **gravestone** or **obituary** written weeks later, every time.

---

## Specific Things to Check

1. **England & Wales civil registration**: The GRO death register entry will name the informant and their relationship. A spouse or child present at the death = primary information. A neighbor or registrar who heard about it = secondary.

2. **Parish burial register**: The burial date is often entered the same day as burial — if one of your records is a burial register, that date is likely the *burial* date, not the death date.

3. **Death certificate vs. burial register**: If you have both, expect them to differ by roughly the burial interval — that's a feature, not a conflict.

This is a great question for genealogical research — Quaker records use this convention consistently, and misreading it causes real dating errors.

## Why Quakers Used Numbered Months

### The Core Religious Reason: Plain Speech

Quakers (the Religious Society of Friends, founded by George Fox in the 1640s–50s) held a testimony of **simplicity and truth** — avoiding anything they considered worldly vanity or falsehood. The names of months and days of the week were, to them, a form of idolatry, because they honored pagan gods:

| Name | Origin |
|---|---|
| January | *Janus* — Roman god of beginnings |
| March | *Mars* — Roman god of war |
| May | *Maia* — Roman goddess |
| June | *Juno* — Roman goddess |
| July | *Julius Caesar* |
| August | *Augustus Caesar* |

The days of the week were equally problematic — Sunday (the Sun), Monday (the Moon), Tuesday (Tiw), Wednesday (Woden), Thursday (Thor), Friday (Frigg/Freya), Saturday (Saturn). All pagan.

Rather than speak names that honored false gods, Quakers simply said **First Month, Second Month…** and **First Day, Second Day…** This was part of the same impulse that led them to use "thee/thou" to everyone (refusing the honorific "you"), refuse to remove their hats before magistrates, and decline to swear oaths.

---

## The Critical Genealogical Complication

Here is where it matters for your research: **the numbering shifted in 1752.**

Before the **Calendar Reform Act of 1750** (which took effect in Britain in **September 1752**), England used the **Julian calendar**, and the legal new year began on **25 March (Lady Day)**. So:

| Quaker "Month" | *Before* 1752 | *After* 1752 |
|---|---|---|
| 1st Month | **March** | January |
| 2nd Month | April | February |
| 3rd Month | May | March |
| 10th Month | December | October |
| 11th Month | January | November |
| 12th Month | February | December |

This is a **double-dated year**, a notation English clerks used because England's legal year began on **25 March (Lady Day)**, not 1 January, until the calendar reform of 1752.

| | Date |
|---|---|

---

February 15 falls in the **1 January – 24 March** window — the awkward overlap period where:
- The **legal/civil year** was still 1750 (the new year hadn't started yet under OS reckoning)
- The **historical/modern year** was already 1751 (because we count from 1 January)

Rather than pick one and risk confusion, careful clerks wrote **both**: `1750/1`. The slash is not uncertainty — it is precision.

---

Use **1751** — always the later (right-hand) year.

---

This double dating only affects the **year**. The **day and month — 15 February — stay exactly as written.** The separate Julian→Gregorian *day* correction (11 days for England) is a different issue; unless you are aligning this date with a Continental record on the Gregorian calendar, you do not need to apply it here.

## What "25 March 1750/1" Means — and Why It's Anomalous

### The double-dating convention (the general rule)

In England before 1752, the legal year began on **25 March (Lady Day)**, not 1 January. To prevent confusion, record-keepers writing dates between **1 January and 24 March** would show *both* years — the Old Style legal year and the New Style year a modern reader would expect:

> "5 February **1750/1**" = 5 Feb **1750** (Old Style) = 5 Feb **1751** (New Style/modern)

The left number is what the clerk's calendar said; the right number is what we'd call it today. Standard practice in modern research notes is to use the New Style year: **1751**.

---

### Why 25 March is a special case ⚠️

**25 March is Lady Day itself — the first day of the new year in Old Style England.** On that date, both the Old Style and New Style years are identical: 25 March 1751 O.S. *is* 25 March 1751 N.S. There is no gap to bridge, so a slash notation on this exact date is **anomalous** — the two years should not differ.

A slash on 25 March typically means one of a few things:
- The clerk was being mechanically cautious and wrote the slash out of habit, even though it wasn't needed
- There is a transcription or copying error (a nearby date, e.g., 24 March, got shifted)
- The register uses an unusual local convention for where the year turns over

---

### What to do before recording the year

> **Do not automatically resolve "25 March 1750/1" to 1751.**

Instead, take this step first:

1. **Look at the surrounding entries in the register.** Find where the year number changes in the sequence of dates. Does the register flip from "1750" to "1751" on 25 March, or does it flip on 1 January? That tells you which convention *this particular clerk* used.
2. If the register clearly turns over on 25 March and the entries just before read "1750," the slash may simply be a scribal caution on the boundary day — in that case, **record it as 25 March 1751** (New Style) with a note.
3. If you cannot inspect surrounding entries, **record the date exactly as written** — `25 March 1750/1` — and add a source note flagging the anomaly.

---

### In your research notes

| Situation | What to record |
|---|---|
| Surrounding register confirms year turns 25 March | `25 March 1751` (note: O.S./N.S. year same; slash anomalous) |
| Cannot verify surrounding context | `25 March 1750/1` *(anomalous double-date; verify in register)* |

The guiding principle: **preserve the ambiguity until the register itself resolves it.** A date recorded with a note is far more defensible than one silently "corrected."
